💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, Nepal's relationship with India was shaped by familiar faces, as leaders of the Himalayan country's erstwhile three major parties took turns in the prime minister's office through revolving coalition governments.
  • This week's state visit to India by Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician, marked a clear break from that pattern.
  • As a young, first-time prime minister with a strong electoral mandate , Shah represents a newly introduced political force in Kathmandu.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, Nepal's relationship with India was shaped by familiar faces, as leaders of the Himalayan country's erstwhile three major parties took turns in the prime minister's office through revolving coalition governments.

This week's state visit to India by Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician, marked a clear break from that pattern.

As a young, first-time prime minister with a strong electoral mandate , Shah represents a newly introduced political force in Kathmandu.

But long-standing economic strain, along with August's devastating flash floods and the Nepalese public's high hopes for more jobs, investment and better governance at home, have made Shah's first bilateral visit abroad more than a mere diplomatic box-ticking exercise.

To safeguard Nepal's flood recovery and development, Shah needs to get off on the right foot with India, his country's southern neighbor and largest trading partner, and its long-standing prime minister, Narendra Modi.

While Nepal and India share an open border as well as deep cultural and historical ties, their relationship has also been marked by territorial disputes and a desire in Nepal to be seen as an equal by its much larger and more powerful neighbor.

Constantino Xavier, a senior fellow at the Center for Social and Economic Progress in Latest Delhi, however, cautioned against expecting too much from a single visit.

"We need a big, long-term ambition coupled with small, short-term steps," he told DW, arguing that economic cooperation should remain the central focus of relations because it directly contributes to the socioeconomic development of both countries.

The young prime minister's test is to turn a strong domestic electoral mandate and political goodwill with Fresh Delhi into tangible economic gain, as well as to address longstanding border disputes and a massive trade imbalance.

Shah's administration sees diplomacy as key to addressing the country's development aspirations, which was reflected in bilateral talks with Modi on Monday.

Economic cooperation featured prominently during the talks as both sides sought engagements in trade, investment, connectivity and infrastructure development.

Kathmandu's priority was securing Indian financial support for reconstruction following the August disaster that claimed the lives of more than 1,450 people, while 5,745 are missing or unaccounted for.

The floods swept away roads, bridges, hydropower projects and settlements, with reconstruction bills estimated at around $4.8 billion (about €4.4 billion).

At a joint press briefing after their talks in Newly introduced Delhi, Modi announced a package of $1.63 billion to help rebuild flood-hit areas and upgrade other infrastructure projects — around $380 million as a grant, with the rest as a concessional loan.

The South Asian neighbors also agreed to deepen cooperation across a wide range of areas, including trade, investment, connectivity and people-to-people ties, and rolled out a new long-term vision aimed at strengthening economic integration and development.

The talks also yielded commitments to broaden educational and innovation partnerships, boost energy and infrastructure cooperation, improve market access and trade links, and enhance landlocked Nepal's connectivity through additional air and port access via India.

Shah's visit offered an opportunity to break the ice in a high-level exchange visit and improve a relationship periodically strained by political mistrust, territorial disputes and differing strategic interests.

Nepal and India both have competing territorial claims over Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura, a strategic Himalayan territory in northwestern Nepal.

Sources indicate that as mayor of Kathmandu, Shah raised the border disputes with India, which helped boost his nationalist image and set his broader political agenda. However, his India visit steered clear of such contentious problems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Foreign Minister of Nepal, mentioned Shah avoided tricky bilateral issues to focus on his administration's economic agenda.

According to recent reports, "This visit could be a good starting point towards resolving the border concerns that have been the key strain in our relations," she told DW. "But the new government didn't show interest or the guts to address this.".

Ashok Swain, head of the Department of Peace and Conflict Research at Sweden's Uppsala University, noted the visit's success should be measured by whether the two countries can establish a predictable and mutually beneficial relationship.

"Nepal's territorial disputes, concerns over the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and its economic and transit dependence on India need to be addressed," Swain told DW.

"Shah's biggest opportunity is to transform Nepal's geographical location between India and China from a strategic vulnerability into an economic and diplomatic asset," he added, arguing that Nepal should not be forced to choose between its two neighbors.

Whether the visit marks a tangible reset on the economic front will ultimately depend not on the number of agreements announced, but on how they are implemented and whether the two governments are willing to address the disputes that have long strained ties.

#162045. Laser Focus at the Top of the World

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (818 w)

Laser Focus at the Top of the World

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.
  • More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors.
  • Since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.

More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a new, more precise method for tracking satellites.

Since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory—laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide.

In 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system officially debuted at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. The observatory’s remote location in the Arctic archipelago is shown in this image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 in July 2026. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth.

It has been revealed that while the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, stated Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s Space Geodesy Project. “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said.

In a recent development, years of development, testing, and careful calibration produced the Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system now running at Ny-Ålesund. Among its features are lasers that can fire pulses thousands of times per second, up from tens of times per second, and sensors that can detect single photons, meaning that less light needs to be reflected back from a satellite.

Recent findings suggest that along with determining the orbits of satellites, SLR is critical for establishing the terrestrial reference frame, the foundation of modern coordinate systems and a common standard that allows measurements to be compared with one another. “If you want to know where your satellite observation is on a map, you need to have it in the proper reference frame,” Merkowitz said. In addition, tracking Earth’s center of mass, measuring changes in sea level and ice mass, studying the motion of tectonic plates, and maintaining global navigation satellite systems such as GPS, all rely on an accurate reference frame.

It has been revealed that the far-north location of the Ny-Ålesund facility improves the distribution of SLR stations across the planet, making the whole network more robust. The location also allows the system to gather more data about polar-orbiting satellites, which include ICESat-2, GRACE-FO, and other Earth observation satellites. “From the station at Goddard [in Greenbelt, Maryland], we’ll catch the polar-orbiting satellites maybe two or three times a day,” Merkowitz said. “But from Ny-Ålesund, you’ll see them almost every orbit.”.

Sources indicate that certain satellite missions may especially benefit from the Arctic location, he added. Take ICESat-2, designed to make precise observations of ice surface heights. Having a station tracking the satellite from an icy polar region could lead to more accurate measurements there. “When it’s over the ice, we want the calibration to be as good as possible,” Merkowitz mentioned.

Industry observers note that innovations and lessons learned from the Svalbard installation will carry over to future ones, Merkowitz said. In particular, the Ny-Ålesund facility drove improvements in automation because the site is located next to a bird sanctuary. Access restrictions require the station to be remotely operated at certain times, such as during the summer breeding season for migratory birds. These capabilities can be refined and applied at other stations. NASA is at the moment building two more next-generation SLR systems to replace legacy instruments at Goddard and the McDonald Geodetic Observatory in Texas.

Industry News: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that at an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today.
  • Industry observers note that the findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes.
  • In a recent development, in a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve crucial biological functions.

In a recent development, in a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

Sources indicate that jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation.

One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

Industry observers note that they found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

In a recent development, this research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal notable new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

Industry observers note that "We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

It has been revealed that he added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject.".

Gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop newly introduced approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

He added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine.".

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island.

Recent findings suggest that jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

Sources indicate that he arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

Today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you thought the Jensen Huang saga was over when he stepped down as Nvidia's CEO, think again.
  • And within hours of Monday's surprise announcement, senators set a date to question him in public — and under oath.
  • Huang, who co-founded chipmaker Nvidia, is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Thursday, Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you thought the Jensen Huang saga was over when he stepped down as Nvidia's CEO, think again. Less than two weeks later, Nvidia gave him his job back.

And within hours of Monday's surprise announcement, senators set a date to question him in public — and under oath.

Huang, who co-founded chipmaker Nvidia, is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 10 a.m. ET, just two days after he's scheduled to speak with various committees of the U.S. House of Representatives. He’s the only witness listed for the hearing, which will focus on U.S. rules limiting where companies can sell their most advanced AI chips. If you want to watch, the committee will be livestreaming the hearing on its website.

Huang has already returned to the Nvidia office, where he was welcomed by cheering employees.

"I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around," he told workers, as seen in a video on X.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, President Trump is taking personal credit for negotiating Huang's return to Nvidia. In a Truth Social post, the president said he assured the Nvidia board that Huang did not pose a national security risk.

According to recent reports, president Trump also posted a picture of Jensen Huang photoshopped into his assassination attempt scene while holding up a red bra with an Nvidia flag in the background. Yes, really.

It has been revealed that the questions about Nvidia's chips go back well before Huang initially stepped down. In 2024, federal investigators began looking into whether Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer based in Singapore, had sent advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That investigation took on new significance when reports surfaced that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, who used to run Megaspeed. Jensen Huang acknowledged the affair, and U.S. authorities suspect Alice Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, according to the New York Times (though China has since denied that she was a spy).

Sources indicate that the newly empowered House Democrats also have questions for Huang, including whether Nvidia interfered with that investigation. In a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, they asked whether his department had allowed Nvidia to intervene in the Megaspeed probe. Lawmakers are also looking into exactly how Huang got his job back and what role the Trump administration played.

Just days before Nvidia brought him back, the board had made clear it had no plans to reinstate him, despite Huang saying he would be "honored" to return. On the tech giant's earnings call on Nov. 17, board chair Harvey Jones even noted, "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

Recent findings suggest that yet, on Nov. 23, the board voted unanimously to do just that. In a statement, the board wrote that it had heard from senior U.S. officials, and "based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk.".

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Harvey Jones said in the statement.

It has been revealed that trump had already signaled he was open to Huang getting his job back. On Nov. 16, he told reporters he "would not mind" if Huang returned as CEO and said Huang had "learned a major lesson.".

Recent findings suggest that by Monday, Trump was taking credit for the decision. He told CNBC he'd pushed Nvidia's board to bring Huang back. Asked whether the board would have done so without him, Trump mentioned, "The answer is no. I believe my intervention was very notable." He also posted on Truth Social, writing, "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World!".

Recent findings suggest that that leaves lawmakers in both parties asking what changed. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called the decision "reckless" and asked the administration to name the officials who spoke to Nvidia and explain what they told the board. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked, "No national security risk? Based on what?" he wrote on X.

Huang had already agreed to answer questions from House lawmakers before he got his job back. That interview is still set for Tuesday, Dec. 1, two days before the public Senate hearing. He’ll meet with three House committees behind closed doors, and the interview will be transcribed.

But now, Huang could also be answering a newly introduced set of questions in public about the affair that helped cost him his job and the president who says he got it back for him. So far, Nvidia and Trump have told their sides of the story. The hearing is a chance to hear Huang's.

Breaking: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing fresh details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System.
  • Fresh research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing fresh details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide vital clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

Fresh research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

Recent findings suggest that the Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Vital Clues.

Dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

"The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan noted.

It has been revealed that "Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth.".

"By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment.".

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts.

To investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

These findings offer a fresh perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

It has been revealed that the implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth.

"The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan stated.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a new era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side.".

Recent findings suggest that the return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.

  • November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know.

November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter.

Recent findings suggest that the Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon, because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee, when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon".

According to recent reports, november's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon.

Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length.

Recent findings suggest that if you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location.

You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering.

Industry observers note that this is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. Check out our full Celestron Nexstar 4SE review for more.

The supermoon will also appear particularly large while close to the horizon, as a phenomenon called the "moon illusion" tricks our brains into thinking that the lunar disk is larger while in the presence of foreground objects compared to when it is overhead.

It'll make for a breathtaking photo opportunity, which you can capitalize on with our beginner's guide to imaging the full moon, along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for capturing the night sky.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has released a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, noted it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

Industry observers note that “We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”.

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based firm had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it noted last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China.

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

Sources indicate that in efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”.

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When India's world chess champion, Dommaraju Gukesh, faced reporters at the pre-tournament press conference in Geneva on Sunday, there was no sign of the youthful, carefree energy one might expect from a 20-year-old.

"I don't think I'm here to defend anything—I'm here to win it all over again," he said.

Starting November 24, Gukesh will be facing challenger Jakhovir Sindarov of Uzbekistan for a purse of $2.5 million (€2.3m) in the World Chess Championship.

It has been revealed that gukesh captured the title in 2024, making him the youngest-ever world champion at just 18. Since then, however, things have not as gone well for the player known for his exceptional calculation skills and a penchant for risky moves. He right now languishes in 26th place in the FIDE world rankings.

Sindarov, who has climbed to number four in the world, told reporters that he only began training "seriously" last year and has learned a lot from observing the reigning world champion.

"He has a very good strength in typical positions, his calculation is very good, and Gukesh can fight until the end," Sindarov said.

Former world champion Viswanathan Anand, who was also one of the world's best players as a teenager, is not completely surprised by Gukesh's lack of form over the past two years.

Recent findings suggest that "He became the world champion (very young). So suddenly the responsibility is shifted onto you and even expectations," Anand told DW.

"Clearly he has deficiencies in his chess as is normal for someone who's 20, he's not had time to experience a lot.".

By the time he became India's first world champion, Anand was 37 – ancient by the age-standards of today's top players.

"With powerful chess software and global connectivity, it is easier for young players today to reach the top level," Jan Gustafsson, coach of Germany's national chess team, told DW.

"Online chess provides many more learning opportunities for talented players," added Gustafsson, who sees the recent movement at the top of the rankings as a "generational shift.".

While Norway's Magnus Carlsen, long considered the greatest player of all time, remains number one in the world rankings, he rarely plays classical chess anymore and gave up his world championship title after declining to defend it in 2023.

Now, young players—particularly from Asia—are pushing to the forefront. Alongside Gukesh and Sindarov, players such as Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa from India and Nodirbek Abdusattorov of Uzbekistan—an emerging chess powerhouse—are considered contenders to win a world championship in the not-too-distant future.

"Broad social acceptance and state support ensure that children can focus on chess at a very early stage," Gustafsson said.

According to recent reports, another contender is Germany's Vincent Keymer, who at 22 is number nine in the world and well established among the world's elite. Most recently, Keymer and his teammates won a bronze medal at the World Team Championship, often referred to as the "Chess Olympiad.".

Tech Report: NASA’s Webb Shows How Supernova Dust Chronicles Star Evolution

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A).
  • Recent findings suggest that this high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb reveals latest details that are helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star.
  • Stars begin their lives as large clouds of mostly hydrogen gas and cosmic dust called molecular clouds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has painted a vibrant tapestry of the legendary supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A). Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a fresh generation of stars and planets.

Recent findings suggest that this high-resolution, mid-infrared observation from Webb reveals latest details that are helping astronomers chronicle the structure and evolution of Cas A’s original star. The Webb data supports a scenario in which the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise. These results published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Stars begin their lives as large clouds of mostly hydrogen gas and cosmic dust called molecular clouds. Eventually, gravity causes these molecular clouds to collapse, the material heats up, and protostars — infant stars — form. Under the constant pressure of gravity, hydrogen within a protostar begins to fuse into helium, which marks the point where protostars evolve into full-fledged stars like our Sun.

As hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats until helium begins to fuse into heavier elements. This process repeats as stars like Cas A’s original star evolve, with increasingly heavier elements fusing in the core (eventually stopping at iron) and lighter elements fusing in surrounding layers. This leads to multiple shells of elements that provide a record of a star’s evolutionary history. When a star goes supernova, these elements are scattered into the surrounding space, where some of them condense to form dust grains, which can clump together. By studying and mapping the composition of these individual, solar-system-sized dust clumps in Cas A, Webb found evidence of a shell merger, a process in which the layers inside a star mix before the explosion.

Industry observers note that “Material within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,” remarked Tea Temim, lead author of the study and research scientist from Columbia University in New York. “So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.”.

For the researchers to know where to look with Webb, they also leveraged data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope. Although it couldn’t resolve the minute details of the region during its observation, Spitzer identified three specific regions to observe with Webb’s keen eye.

According to recent reports, two of the targets were inside Cas A’s reverse-shocked region, where an inward-moving shock wave collides with debris thrown outward by the supernova. Webb observed that the ejecta in one of the two contained mostly silica dust, while the other was dominated by carbon dust. The third target was the “Green Monster,” a structure first discovered by Webb, which was found to be rich in complex magnesium silicates. Unlike the other two regions, the Green Monster originated from material the star shed before it exploded, rather than from the supernova’s ejecta.

Building on the X-ray observations of NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the JAXA-led XRISM, Webb mapped the dust composition of Cas A across the entire remnant, providing crucial insight into the shell merger phenomenon. Together, these observations indicate that the merger was underway very shortly before the supernova explosion.

“With Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,” noted Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana. “As a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. It’s telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.”.

The dust map from Webb also reveals that the merger signatures are present throughout much of the supernova remnant. These efforts provide a new method for other astronomers who want to infer characteristics about an originating star’s structure by using the dust of a supernova remnant.

The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the company's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

According to recent reports, when "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

Industry observers note that the company aims to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said on the tech giant's earnings call earlier this month.

In a recent development, paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

The earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be important as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The organization has said it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

Breaking: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, newly introduced research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors.
  • It has been revealed that the discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas.
  • Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, newly introduced research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors. The findings also raise questions about a familiar feature of the Milky Way, suggesting that part of what astronomers have long considered a spiral arm may actually be something else.

It has been revealed that the discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas. These waves squeeze the gas together, creating conditions that allow fresh stars to form in a region where such intense forces usually prevent their birth.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.

Industry observers note that lead author Dr. Hillary Davis, who recently completed her PhD at the University of Sydney's School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy, remarked the research provides new insights into the structures near the galactic center and how gas moves around them.

Sources indicate that "At its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale," Dr. Davis said.

"In most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. What's extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed.".

A Hidden Star Factory at the Heart of the Milky Way.

Sources indicate that the Milky Way belongs to a class of galaxies known as barred spiral galaxies. Unlike galaxies with only a central concentration of stars and surrounding spiral arms, these systems contain an elongated structure of stars stretching across their central region. In our galaxy, this structure is called the Galactic bar.

As the bar rotates, its gravity influences nearby gas, driving it into powerful shock fronts. These fronts compress the gas in much the same way that a shock wave compresses air.

Sources indicate that studying this structure from Earth is particularly difficult because we are located inside the Milky Way rather than viewing it from the outside. Large amounts of cosmic dust also block our view of the galactic center.

Industry observers note that "The Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view," Dr. Davis noted.

"As a result, the bar's properties have been highly debated.".

Recent findings suggest that observations of other barred galaxies have shown that these shock fronts generally inhibit the formation of fresh stars, even in regions containing abundant gas. The intense conditions make it difficult for the gas to collapse into stars.

However, the newly introduced findings indicate that the Milky Way may behave differently. Although it is not the only known example, our galaxy appears to belong to a relatively small group in which substantial star formation takes place along the shock fronts of the central bar.

"We believe that the Milky Way's bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies," Dr. Davis said.

A Milky Way Spiral Arm May Not Be What It Seems.

To investigate this unusual activity, the research team compared detailed computer simulations showing how galaxies change over billions of years with astronomical observations of regions where massive stars are forming.

It has been revealed that A crucial part of the evidence came from masers, naturally occurring sources that emit highly concentrated microwave radiation. These emissions are associated with the formation of massive stars and operate on a principle similar to lasers, but at microwave wavelengths.

By examining the positions of these masers, the researchers uncovered a striking match between actual observations and the locations of shock fronts predicted by their simulations.

"We found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations," Dr. Davis said. "This suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar.

"This raises questions about the Galaxy's spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation," she said.

Recent findings suggest that the possibility is significant because it suggests that some of the star formation previously attributed to the Norma spiral arm could instead be occurring along the central bar. If confirmed, this interpretation would change how astronomers understand the arrangement of stars and gas in that part of the Milky Way.

Latest Evidence Could Redraw the Milky Way's Map.

Beyond revealing an unusual location for star birth, the research also sheds light on the physical properties of the Galactic bar itself.

Astronomers have debated the structure's length, orientation, and rotation speed for decades, partly because the Milky Way's dust and our viewing position make direct measurements so challenging.

Recent findings suggest that "Our findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar," Dr. Davis noted.

The team's analysis indicates that the bar extends approximately 4.3 kiloparsecs, equivalent to about 14,000 light-years, outward from the galactic center along its long axis. This supports a picture of the Milky Way containing a relatively long bar that rotates slowly.

The results illustrate how increasingly sophisticated simulations can help scientists investigate regions of our galaxy that are difficult to observe directly. By comparing models spanning billions of years with the available astronomical evidence, researchers can narrow down the possible structures and processes shaping the Milky Way.

"By comparing a fresh generation of large-scale computerized galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way," Dr. Davis remarked.

In a recent development, the authors reported no competing interests. Research funding came from the Australian Research Council, the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish National Space Agency, the LMK Foundation and eSSENCE (Sweden).

Computing resources and data storage were provided through National Computing Infrastructure Australia, an NCRIS capability supported by the Australian Government, and LUNARC, the Centre for Scientific and Technical Computing at Lund University, Sweden.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of Europa Clipper’s journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the release of the agency’s newest documentary, “The Europa Concept.”.
  • According to recent reports, the documentary will air on NASA+, the NASA app, and the agency’s website starting Monday, Nov.
  • It took decades of science, thousands of dedicated minds, endless creativity, and a whole lot of grit to get the Europa Clipper spacecraft to the launch pad in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of Europa Clipper’s journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the release of the agency’s newest documentary, “The Europa Concept.”.

According to recent reports, the documentary will air on NASA+, the NASA app, and the agency’s website starting Monday, Nov. 23, and is coming soon to YouTube.

It took decades of science, thousands of dedicated minds, endless creativity, and a whole lot of grit to get the Europa Clipper spacecraft to the launch pad in 2024. Now the orbiter, the largest NASA has ever sent into deep space, is two years into its five-year, 1.8 billion-mile (2.9 billion-kilometer) journey to the Jupiter system, where it will conduct flybys of Europa in search of the conditions for life in the vast ocean thought to hide beneath the moon’s icy surface.

Recent findings suggest that “The things we will learn from Europa Clipper will be so sensational, so fantastic, that everyone will be screaming for the next mission,” stated Curt Niebur, program scientist in the Planetary Science Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “The only thing that matters is that we learn enough that we, in the broadest sense, want to do it again somewhere else — because that’s what exploration is.”.

In a recent development, following a team of dedicated engineers and scientists on their yearslong efforts, the documentary captures how they developed a mission to Europa and built a spacecraft capable of surviving one of the most punishing radiation environments in our solar system. A product of Jupiter’s powerful magnetic field, that same radiation may have contributed to creating a potentially habitable environment on Europa.

Industry observers note that the moon, an object of fascination since its discovery by Galileo Galilei in 1610, only began to reveal its secrets with data obtained by NASA’s Pioneer 10 in 1973, followed the next year by Pioneer 11. But humanity didn’t get its first detailed look at Europa until Voyager 1’s flyby in 1979. More detailed glimpses of the moon followed from the agency’s Voyager 2, Galileo, Cassini, and Juno missions, each helping illuminate the way for Europa Clipper.

Work officially began on the mission at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California in 2013, initiating an 11-year trek to build the spacecraft and its suite of nine science instruments in time to launch during a specific period of planetary alignment. Along the way, the team encountered plenty of unforeseen challenges, including a global pandemic and, just before launch on Oct. 14, 2024, a Category 5 hurricane and tornadoes near NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

“With Europa Clipper, we’ve taken the next step in solar system exploration, which will help us uncover the mysteries of an ocean world, and ultimately, whether potentially habitable worlds beyond our own exist,” said Jordan Evans, director of flight projects at JPL and the mission’s previous project manager. “This documentary pays tribute to the ingenuity, teamwork, and dedication that continue to make this incredible mission possible.”.

“The Europa Concept” takes audiences through the highs and lows alongside the thousands more who made Europa Clipper’s journey to the launch pad a success — and who will, in the coming years, be there to share the mission’s findings about humanity’s place in the cosmos.

Find “The Europa Concept” on NASA+ here:.

https://plus.nasa.gov/video/the-europa-concept/.

Managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, JPL leads the development of the Europa Clipper mission in partnership with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, for NASA. The main spacecraft body was designed by APL in collaboration with JPL and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, and NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The Planetary Missions Program Office at NASA Marshall executes program management of the Europa Clipper mission. NASA’s Launch Services Program, based at Kennedy, managed the launch service for the Europa Clipper spacecraft.

Find more information about Europa Clipper here:.

Breaking: Mysterious fresh viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history.
  • In a recent development, the research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins.
  • The discovery could have important implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and tiny protein compartments inside cells, offering latest clues about how some of life's earliest biological structures may have developed.

In a recent development, the research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins. Scientists previously believed these compartments evolved from viruses. However, the fresh evidence suggests a more complicated evolutionary relationship in which viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

The discovery could have important implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life. It also raises the possibility that viruses have biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.

Mysterious New Viruses Reveal an Evolutionary Connection.

In a recent development, at the center of the discovery are proteins that fold into a distinctive three-dimensional structure known as the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are found in both viruses and encapsulins.

Industry observers note that the newly identified viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. They also possess characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, making them possible evolutionary intermediates between the two. Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared.

It has been revealed that "What makes the HK97-fold proteins so interesting is that they can form shells that enclose biochemical reactions in cellular lineages, archaea, and bacteria. But they also serve genetic purposes in viruses, storing and protecting their viral genome," said Abelardo Aguilar, the study's first author and a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami College of Arts and Sciences.

"These proteins build compartments with two different roles, which connects directly with the study of the origin of life and its early evolution because if you think about it, life at its core is about enclosing reactions and also enclosing information that can be inherited so those reactions can happen in the future.".

AI Helps Discover Hidden Viruses in Billions of DNA Sequences.

According to recent reports, to uncover these previously unknown viruses, Aguilar worked with Antoni Luque Santolaria, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Biology. Luque also holds secondary appointments in the Department of Physics within the College of Arts and Sciences and the Department of Chemical, Environmental and Materials Engineering in the College of Engineering. The project brought together collaborators from multiple institutions.

Rather than relying on laboratory experiments to grow viruses, the team searched enormous genetic databases containing billions of DNA sequences. They combined bioinformatics, models of protein behavior, and artificial intelligence tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, to investigate the structures encoded by these sequences.

The databases included IMG/M, a resource associated with the U.S. Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute and the University of California, Berkeley. Its genetic information comes from environmental samples collected around the world, including soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut, and numerous other locations.

This approach allows scientists to investigate viruses that have never been successfully grown in a laboratory, greatly expanding the number of organisms and evolutionary relationships they can study.

According to recent reports, "The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab. But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don't know the host, that we can't culture in the lab, but that are everywhere," Luque explained. "That means there are multiple questions in relation to evolution and how viruses have adapted to the world that it's now possible to explore bioinformatically.".

Viral Protein Shells May Have Unexpected Functions.

Beyond identifying the latest viruses, the researchers proposed a possible molecular explanation for how viruses and encapsulins could have evolved from one another.

Recent findings suggest that their model centers on procapsids, immature viral protein shells (capsids) that may provide a pathway between the two types of structures. These shells could potentially support both genetic functions, such as containing viral DNA, and metabolic functions involving chemical reactions.

According to recent reports, this raises an intriguing possibility. Viral capsids are generally recognized for packaging and protecting genetic material, but certain forms might also help create environments where biochemical reactions can occur.

"One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole," Aguilar explained.

Although further research is needed to establish these potential functions, the findings suggest that scientists may need to look beyond the infectious stages of viruses to fully understand their roles in nature.

"When we're looking at viruses, we tend to look only at the particles that are infective, and this study points out that we might need to start putting more emphasis on the non-infective versions of the virus and what other functions those viral-like particles may have that we have overlooked in the past.".

Newly introduced AI Tools Open the Door to More Viral Discoveries.

Industry observers note that the research also demonstrates how artificial intelligence and computational biology are transforming the study of viruses. By combining powerful analytical tools with knowledge of protein structure and physical behavior, scientists can now investigate evolutionary questions that were previously difficult to explore.

Sources indicate that supported by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and the U.S. National Science Foundation, the project provides a framework for studying other poorly understood viruses and their biological capabilities.

The researchers believe these methods could also be useful beyond evolutionary biology, including efforts to understand newly emerging viruses and pathogens.

According to recent reports, "If you have the right question and you pair it with the right tools and physical insights, it gives researchers an opportunity to look at viruses in a way that we didn't have an opportunity to do before," Luque said. "There are evolution questions, but there are also questions about emerging pathogens or emerging viruses. The set of tools that we use can be moved forward in different contexts.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Twitter’s traditional bird icon was booted and replaced with an image of a Shiba Inu, an apparent nod to dogecoin, the joke cryptocurrency that CEO Elon Musk is being sued over.

Musk addressed the change Monday afternoon, tweeting, “as promised” above an image of a year-old conversation in which another user suggested that Musk “just buy Twitter” and “change the bird logo to a doge.”.

Elon Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out one account.

The doge logo appeared on the site two days after Musk asked a judge to throw out a $258 billion racketeering lawsuit accusing him of running a pyramid scheme to support the dogecoin, according to Reuters.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”.

It wasn’t clear whether the logo change was permanent. Musk has been known to use Twitter to troll both his fans and his critics.

The price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

Dogecoin was created December 6, 2013, by a pair of software engineers — as a joke. The name is a nod to the “doge” meme that became popular a decade ago. Its Shiba Inu mascot mimicks that meme: a dog surrounded by a bunch of Comic Sans text in broken English.

  • Sources indicate that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them.
  • According to recent reports, the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does.
  • Revision, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

According to recent reports, the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another substantial provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Revision, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and mentioned that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

Sources indicate that to test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:.

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”.

Recent findings suggest that although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router to another one. Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:.

In a recent development, each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Sources indicate that parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

In a recent development, secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were promptly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:.

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically revealed up two or three days after the request.

Recent findings suggest that this wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher noted he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

After Japan's APEC snub, what's next for its China ties?
