💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.
  • After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.
  • It has been revealed that it may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.

After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.

It has been revealed that it may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.

Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.

"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," noted William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.

"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.

Yang added that the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations.".

China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.

Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.

Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.

Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.

The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.

Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.

According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury.

China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.

And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with indicates of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.

"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," mentioned Adebahr.

"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it.".

Industry observers note that adebahr added that this left China with little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise. However, he pointed out that Beijing's reliance on coercion could backfire by prompting Japan to increase defence spending and seek closer ties with other partners.

Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, remarked analyst Yang.

As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.

Sources indicate that "This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan.".

"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he remarked.

Yang added that Japan was likely to seek opportunities to signal goodwill and improve relations "in return for small-scale compromises." However, he remarked that a reset in the dynamics would depend on how the Trump administration shaped its foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

Analyst Adebahr noted that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.

In a recent development, "I would not be too pessimistic about the relationship, because in the medium term, trade, technology and critical minerals are now seen as security issues," he added. "Therefore, complex interdependence will prevent a return to the old pattern of keeping politics and economics separate.".

"While economic interdependence alone will not be enough to stabilize the relationship, full decoupling is highly unlikely, as transaction costs would be far too high for both sides," he mentioned.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be a small fission power system that will generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 16 average U.S.
  • NASA aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and operate it on the Moon for at least five years after deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA is seeking industry partners to develop and test the first nuclear reactor designed to provide electricity on the Moon, a major step toward establishing a sustained human presence on the lunar surface.

In a recent development, lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be a small fission power system that will generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 16 average U.S. households annually on Earth. For NASA’s intends for a Moon Base, that energy could support future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and other essential infrastructure.

NASA aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and operate it on the Moon for at least five years after deployment.

Sources indicate that unlike solar power, which depends on sunlight, a nuclear reactor can generate electricity continuously, including during the Moon’s approximately two-week-long nights. This capability will enable future lunar operations, particularly in locations where sunlight is limited or unavailable.

It has been revealed that “This request for proposals represents an notable step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” mentioned Brian Giblin, NASA’s Lunar Reactor-1 program manager. “A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface. Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.”.

Industry observers note that NASA’s Space Power and Reactor Capabilities Request for Proposals incorporates feedback received after the agency released a draft proposal in August and hosted an industry day in September at the Ohio Aerospace Institute in Cleveland. The solicitation requires that the reactor must meet Department of Energy (DOE) safety standards for nuclear operations.

While the primary purpose of the Request for Proposals is to advance the technology, testing, and flight design of LR-1, NASA may problem additional task orders to support the development of other space nuclear power systems. Proposals are due by Dec. 21.

According to recent reports, nuclear power will be increasingly key to NASA’s space exploration ambitions. Lunar nights last about 14 Earth days, while dust storms on Mars can block sunlight for months. Farther from the Sun, solar power becomes progressively less effective. Nuclear systems offer a reliable source of electricity in these challenging environments.

According to recent reports, LR-1 is managed by the agency’s Space Reactors Division in partnership with the Department of Energy. The division is also responsible for the development of NASA’s Space Reactor‑1 (SR-1) Freedom. Scheduled to launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom will deliver three SkyFall helicopters to Mars and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion, which uses electricity generated by a nuclear reactor to power spacecraft propulsion systems. This technology could enable future spacecraft to travel farther and undertake deep space missions that aren’t possible using conventional propulsion.

In a recent development, together, LR-1 and SR-1 Freedom are advancing nuclear power and propulsion technologies to enable a fresh era of space exploration. By investing in these technologies, NASA and DOE are helping secure America’s leadership in space for decades to come.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman.
  • Industry observers note that verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex.
  • It has been revealed that the Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman. The ruler, known as Verica, played a pivotal role in events leading to the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43. The findings challenge longstanding assumptions about early British history and the political influence of women during this period.

Industry observers note that verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex. Around AD 40, Verica was forced from power and escaped to Rome, where the exiled ruler sought assistance from Emperor Claudius.

It has been revealed that the Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain. If this account is accurate, Verica's actions may have helped set in motion one of the most consequential events in British history.

Ancient Evidence Challenges an Iron Age King's Identity.

Industry observers note that dr. Miles Russell, Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University, led the research and argues that earlier historians incorrectly identified Verica as male.

"Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female.".

Industry observers note that russell points to several pieces of evidence supporting this interpretation. One is the name Verica itself, which ends in the letter "a," a feature common among female names of the time. Other prominent examples include Cartimandua, who ruled the Brigantes (in Yorkshire), and Boudica, leader of the Iceni (in Norfolk).

All three rulers lived during roughly the same period. Boudica is the best known because of her rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60. However, Russell argues that Verica may have held even greater political power and influence.

Another notable clue comes from coins issued under Verica's rule. These coins bear the Latin title "rex," traditionally translated as "king," which has contributed to the assumption that Verica was male. Russell explains that the title was not necessarily restricted to men.

"People also assume she was a 'he' because of the term 'rex' on coins, but rex is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous.".

He continued: "The use of the Latin title rex on coins demonstrates that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor.".

Sources indicate that the artwork on Verica's coins provides another intriguing clue. Rather than depicting the masculine warriors commonly featured on coins produced by other British Iron Age rulers, Verica's coins show a figure with distinctly feminine characteristics.

"Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback.".

The Forgotten Ruler Behind Rome's Invasion of Britain.

It has been revealed that russell believes Verica's importance extended far beyond the ruler's identity. He argues that Verica may have been instrumental in helping Claudius successfully invade Britain.

Recent findings suggest that ancient Roman writers frequently portrayed Claudius as an ineffective emperor who was easily influenced by women and formerly enslaved people who had gained their freedom. This reputation may have shaped how historians described Verica's role in persuading him to invade.

Russell suggests that Cassius Dio's account reinforced this negative portrayal by presenting the invasion as a decision made under the influence of a woman. In reality, he argues, Verica may have been a valuable political and military ally who supplied the Romans with intelligence and practical assistance.

In a recent development, "The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked. In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica's role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her on board ensured the project was a success, as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.

"The invasion was Claudius' great triumph -- it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it.".

For Claudius, the conquest of Britain offered an opportunity to establish his reputation as a successful military commander. Verica's removal from power gave him a political justification for intervening, while the exiled ruler's knowledge of Britain may have helped the Roman forces achieve their objectives.

Could Rome's Conquest of Britain Have Been Avoided?

Although Verica was an key political figure in late Iron Age Britain, the ruler's influence has received relatively little attention compared with that of other prominent leaders.

In a recent development, russell believes the archaeological evidence supports recognizing Verica as one of Britain's earliest and most significant female rulers. He also raises the possibility that the Roman invasion might never have occurred without Verica's exile and subsequent appeal to Claudius.

In a recent development, "We should take the archaeological evidence at face value" says Russell "and remember Verica as a female-king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed, fleeing to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place.".

New Insights Into Women in Iron Age Britain.

The findings build on earlier Bournemouth University research exploring the position of women in ancient British society.

According to recent reports, last year, a study involving Russell and other BU researchers uncovered evidence of a matriarchal society in Iron Age Britain. The research indicated that husbands moved into their wives' communities after marriage, suggesting that women occupied a central position in the social structure.

Together, these discoveries are prompting researchers to reconsider the influence women may have exercised in Iron Age Britain, both within their communities and in the political decisions that shaped the region's future.

It has been revealed that russell's research on Verica is presented in the upcoming book Caratacus: Great king of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902). The findings are also discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By now, anyone reading this has probably gotten themselves a PS5 or Xbox and played at least a handful of hours of Grand Theft Auto VI after it launched last week. Next time you go to play the game on your console of choice, there will likely be a patch you have to download.

In a recent development, on Monday, Rockstar released the first official post-launch patch for GTA 6. It's not a hugely seismic patch by any means, as it largely addresses a handful of in-game glitches that range from minor to major. Since GTA 6 is not a multiplayer game, you might be able to play it without downloading the patch, but based on the patch notes, you will probably want to wait for it to install first.

Industry observers note that according to Rockstar's enhancement notes, the first GTA 6 patch is intended to fix seven common bugs players had encountered in the first few days after launch. Here are all the things Rockstar noted it fixed on Monday:.

"Several complications" that had caused the game to crash.

An problem that caused weather to not change for extended periods of time.

An issue where the game would not auto-save correctly.

"Several problems" that caused in-game phone calls, including ones that push the story forward, to not trigger on time.

An glitch where players could not lose their wanted levels.

An issue where players could not deadlift at the gym.

An matter that caused partner characters to not hand bags of contraband to the player.

As you can see, these range from minor irritations to nearly game-breaking glitches. Phone calls not triggering properly is especially bad, as they regularly unlock upcoming story missions. Obviously, not being able to lose a wanted level would also be a pretty major bummer.

HBO Max — top pick for premium content.

Disney+ — best for families.

Peacock — low-cost choice for live sport.

Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
  • In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.
  • “We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”.

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

In a recent development, the HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet declared whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey.

“It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”.

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

The accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

It has been revealed that “They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party declared support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake.

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” noted Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”.

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, remarked Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”.

Somer said that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she noted. “It’s a matter of survival.”.

Ozsoy says his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

It has been revealed that “We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker mentioned.

Two women arrested for not wearing hijab following ‘yogurt attack’.

Two women were arrested in Iran for failing to wear the hijab in public, after a man threw a tub of yogurt at them at a store in the city of Shandiz on Thursday, according to Mizan News Agency, the state-run outlet for Iran’s judiciary.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts.

In a recent development, oil prices spiked Monday after OPEC+ producers unexpectedly declared that they would cut output. Brent crude, the global benchmark, jumped 5.31% to $84.13 a barrel, while WTI, the US benchmark, rose 5.48% to $79.83. Both were the sharpest price rises in almost a year. The collective output cut by the nine members of OPEC+ totals 1.66 million barrels per day.

Iran blames Israel for the killing of second IRGC officer, vows to respond.

According to recent reports, A second Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) officer died following an attack in Syria on Friday, according to Iranian state media on Sunday. Iranian state media noted the Iranian military adviser died after an Israeli attack near the Syrian capital Damascus left him wounded. The attack also killed another IRGC officer. In a tweet on Sunday, Iranian government spokesman Ali Bahadori Jahromi said the alleged Israeli attack wouldn’t go unanswered. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Nasser Kanaani said on Sunday that Iran has the right to respond to “state terrorism.”.

Iranian-American comedian Maz Jobrani, who has been touring the Middle East, spoke to CNN’s Becky Anderson about his support for the protests in his homeland, saying that he used his standup comedy platform to highlight the “brutality against the Iranian people.”.

“It was an opportunity for me to say, ‘let’s keep fighting,’” he said.

An Iranian state news outlet is gloating at what it sees as the demise of the US dollar.

IRNA recreated a popular meme to mark China and Brazil’s decision to reportedly ditch the US dollar as an intermediary in trade, citing the Chinese state news outlet, China Daily. It highlights two men representing China and Brazil posing in front of a grave labelled “USD.”.

It has been revealed that the meme was pinned to the top of IRNA’s Twitter page, and was met with laughter and ridicule. “Dream on,” remarked another user, pointing to the dollar’s use as the main reserve currency around the world.

China Daily stated that the agreement was part of “the rising global use of the Chinese renminbi.” It would reportedly enable China and Brazil to conduct trade and financial transactions using local currencies instead of the dollar.

#162011. Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1074 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today.
  • According to recent reports, two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation.
  • According to recent reports, scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For billions of years, Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen, making the planet vastly different from the world we know today. A new scientific analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere during three major stages, while the deep oceans took much longer to catch up. In some cases, the delay stretched across hundreds of millions of years, with the final transition involving a gap of roughly 600 million years.

According to recent reports, two geochemists from Chengdu University of Technology have presented this revised timeline in The Innovation. Their findings challenge the traditional understanding of Earth's oxygen history by examining chemical evidence that reflects conditions in the ancient atmosphere rather than relying primarily on measurements of ocean chemistry.

Ancient Rocks Reveal a Different Oxygen Timeline.

According to recent reports, scientists have traditionally reconstructed Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels using chemical clues preserved in ancient ocean sediments. However, the amount of oxygen in seawater is influenced by many factors besides the atmosphere, including nutrient availability, biological productivity, ocean circulation, and the shapes of ocean basins. This makes ocean chemistry an imperfect guide to conditions in the air.

The researchers instead focused on sulfate, a chemical compound that can preserve a distinctive signal from atmospheric oxygen. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere produce an unusual shortage of the oxygen isotope oxygen-17. When sulfide minerals undergo weathering, this chemical fingerprint is transferred into sulfate, which can eventually become preserved in sedimentary rocks. By examining these signatures, scientists can gain a more direct picture of how atmospheric oxygen changed over time.

It has been revealed that according to this evidence, Earth's first major increase in oxygen occurred during the Great Oxidation Event, between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago. Atmospheric oxygen rose from less than one-millionth of today's concentration to somewhere between 0.1% and 10% of modern levels.

The second major increase took place approximately 1.3 billion to 1.0 billion years ago, followed by a third between 440 million and 410 million years ago. Both occurred earlier than conventional timelines suggest.

Under this interpretation, the well-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, traditionally dated to 800 million to 500 million years ago and 420 million to 360 million years ago, mainly reflect delayed changes in ocean oxygen levels. The oceans responded roughly 200 million and 30 million years after the corresponding atmospheric increases.

Earth's Atmosphere and Oceans Did Not Always Change Together.

Recent findings suggest that despite these major increases, oxygen remained relatively scarce throughout much of Earth's history. Models based on the isotope evidence suggest that atmospheric oxygen during the middle Proterozoic reached only about 0.1% to 1% of present-day levels.

Another clue comes from the fossil record of charcoal. Because charcoal formation requires atmospheric oxygen concentrations of approximately three-quarters of modern levels, its absence from older rocks suggests that oxygen remained too scarce to support widespread burning. Charcoal first appears in the geological record around 420 million years ago.

The researchers also highlight a surprising relationship between oxygen in the atmosphere and oxygen in the oceans. Over extremely long periods, the two generally increased together. However, on timescales of around a million years, they could move in opposite directions.

When additional oxygen entered the oceans, it could react with accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, consuming oxygen in the process. These reactions could reduce the amount of oxygen remaining in the atmosphere.

Industry observers note that as a result, some chemical signals previously interpreted as evidence of rising oxygen may actually record periods when atmospheric oxygen was declining. This possibility could change how scientists interpret major fluctuations in Earth's ancient oxygen record.

Oxygen-Rich Oases Existed Billions of Years Ago.

The spread of oxygen through Earth's oceans was also far from uniform. The researchers describe two major sources of oxygen in seawater: oxygen produced locally by photosynthetic microorganisms and oxygen absorbed from the atmosphere.

Sources indicate that the first process created isolated pockets of oxygen-rich water as early as 3 billion years ago, possibly even earlier. These small oxygenated environments existed during the Archean, when the atmosphere and most of the oceans still contained very little free oxygen.

Industry observers note that as atmospheric oxygen levels gradually increased, oxygen entering seawater from the air became more key. Eventually, this atmospheric supply overtook local biological production as the dominant mechanism driving widespread ocean oxygenation.

According to recent reports, even then, the transformation was remarkably slow. According to the proposed timeline, the deep ocean did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago, long after oxygen had begun accumulating in the atmosphere.

How Rising Oxygen Changed the Evolution of Life.

These findings also offer a new perspective on the relationship between oxygen and the evolution of complex organisms.

Recent findings suggest that when Earth's atmosphere contained virtually no oxygen, its absence placed a major restriction on oxygen-dependent life. During the Proterozoic, increasing oxygen availability gradually made latest environments accessible, although concentrations continued to fluctuate as early animals evolved.

Rather than acting as a single trigger for complex life, oxygen initially provided opportunities for biological innovation. Only after the third major atmospheric increase did higher oxygen levels become a powerful force supporting greater biological complexity.

This later transformation helped create conditions favorable for larger animals, more active predators, and organisms capable of occupying deeper marine environments.

The researchers acknowledge that notable uncertainties remain. The available isotope record does not capture every change in detail, and absolute atmospheric oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain difficult to establish. Additional increases or decreases may have occurred without leaving sufficiently clear chemical evidence to identify them.

Nevertheless, the analysis proposes a major revision to the sequence of events that transformed Earth into an oxygen-rich planet. Rather than the oceans becoming oxygenated first and the atmosphere following, the evidence suggests that atmospheric oxygen increased well before the deep oceans responded.

That prolonged delay may have played an crucial role in shaping the environments where complex life emerged and evolved.

Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
  • It has been revealed that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S.
  • Apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.

It has been revealed that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.

Apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.

It's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.

Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.

"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," said Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.

Fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves swiftly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out upcoming garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.

"We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," stated U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20.".

But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.

The average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.

When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.

"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," said Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.

Though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.

Industry observers note that sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She said that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.

Sources indicate that "There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman said. "But I think both these trends are conflated.".

According to recent reports, nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.

Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.

It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.

In a recent development, apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, remarked BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.

Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.

"Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," stated Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics.".

Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.

Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, said China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

"They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," said Lu.

AlixPartners' Lapinsky remarked these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.

"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," mentioned BTIG's Stichter.

And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also mentioned she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.

Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.

According to recent reports, ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the tech giant said it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.

Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.

The brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report. Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.

Alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.

Recent findings suggest that shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices. The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge.

Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It has been revealed that though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky said worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the firm is doing well.

"What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," mentioned AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
  • Recent findings suggest that the firm’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta.
  • “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Major Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

Recent findings suggest that the firm’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”.

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

In a recent development, but all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the firm’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

It has been revealed that that would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and Newly introduced Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing newly introduced renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

In a recent development, still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”.

It would very much be in the public interest for other Major Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past month, tech outages have disrupted work emails, delayed bank transactions, and temporarily grounded departing flights across the United States. Most of the biggest disruptions happened within six days of one another.

On Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton remarked Americans should expect more disruptions like these, but not because of an incoming cyberattack; rather, because companies and government agencies are now in the process of updating aging technology.

It has been revealed that "We are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service," Clayton told CNN's State of the Union on Sunday, Nov. 24. "That is going to happen." He said much of the country's digital infrastructure was built over three decades or more and needs upgrades to run better and stay secure. (As one example, the FAA is still in the process of phasing out floppy disks, with a target of retiring the '90s-era technology by 2028.).

Clayton compared it to weekend maintenance at work: A company might take a system offline on Saturday and strategy to have it back by 2 A.M. Sunday. If the team finds another problem during the upgrade, it might be Sunday afternoon before the system is back up. "We are taking more systems down and putting them back up than ever before," he mentioned.

It was a lot to keep track of in six days: On Nov. 12, some Microsoft Outlook consumers couldn't open their inboxes or send email. A day later, the Federal Aviation Administration paused departures nationwide after air traffic control communications problems. Then, on Nov. 16, a software bug delayed Chase transactions, and a separate outage briefly paused United Airlines departures. The following day, several Apple services ran into problems, and the National Security Agency's classified internal network went offline.

Sources indicate that as Mashable has reported, despite the odd timing, the outages were not related, and Clayton told ABC's This Week that they were neither coordinated nor related to state-sponsored cyberattacks either. He attributed the disruptions to system upgrades he called "absolutely necessary going forward." "And we’re going to see more of that," he mentioned. He also said, "The need to improve our digital infrastructure is clear.".

AI is identifying zero-day bugs in software faster than ever, and fixing those flaws safely takes time. Some zero-day bug bounty programs have been forced to shut down entirely, and earlier this year, the Zero Day Initiative reported bug reports had increased 490 percent year over year. Companies now have to move swiftly to patch all the upcoming bugs found by AI.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft President Brad Smith called the pressure to move faster part of the "AI ripple effects" on CBS's Face the Nation on Nov. 22 — companies want to fix flaws before attackers can use them. On older systems, Smith stated, moving that promptly can leave engineers with less time to test what happens when a fix goes live.

Recent findings suggest that dmitri Alperovitch, chair of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, described what that looks like for the people doing the work. "I.T. teams, network teams are overwhelmed. They're working 24/7. They're making mistakes," he remarked on the same program. He expects more outages as teams work through the growing number of flaws they've found.

In a recent development, the National Security Agency's outage offers one example of how an urgent fix can disrupt service. The agency's classified internal network went offline on Nov. 17 during work after the agency installed a security fix for PHP, a widely used programming language, Clayton told Fox Business. Those same flaws, known as P2PSHELL, had already forced some website operators to take their sites offline in October while they installed the fix, as Mashable reported at the time. OpenAI noted that its GPT-5.6 Sol model had found the bugs.

In a recent development, microsoft, on the other hand, traced its outage to a software bug introduced in July that went unnoticed for months. It only became a problem in November, when Microsoft sent more Teams traffic to servers that also handle Outlook email. Some of those servers were already offline, and the extra traffic triggered the bug on others. When those servers stopped responding, Microsoft automatically sent traffic to the ones that were still working. They started to fail, too.

Smith remarked the broader work could take months. His advice? Everyone should install security updates as soon they arrive on a phone or laptop.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites.

The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million. The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042. The work will take place at the awardee’s facility.

Sources indicate that under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, is managing the acquisition, and NOAA will own and operate the instruments and deliver the data to consumers worldwide. Microwave sounders provide critical measurements of temperature and moisture in the atmosphere, which significantly influence weather patterns. The SMBA instruments could improve the medium-range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service.

The NEON mission is a collaboration between NASA and NOAA. The mission is led by NOAA, which provides funding, technical requirements, and postlaunch operations. NASA will manage the development of the NEON satellites and launch them for NOAA. NASA and NOAA will work with commercial partners to design and build the NEON spacecraft and instruments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.
  • The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031.
  • According to recent reports, FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the event twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.

According to recent reports, FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so dominant, securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.

"We expect and blueprint for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.

The 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham noted the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country.".

Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable advance for the women's game. The 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.

Recent findings suggest that the next World Cup will be in Brazil in 2027, running from June 24 to July 25. . Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany.

#162003. Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1267 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Substantial Bang.
  • An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history.
  • Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Substantial Bang. Each is powered by an enormous black hole that somehow grew to an astonishing size when the Universe was still in its infancy. Scientists have no definitive explanation for how these two cosmic giants became so massive so quickly. The remarkable pair has been given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history. Officially designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the pair also holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from the early period known as cosmic dawn.

Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult. Discovering two so close together, especially from such an early period in the Universe's history, makes this finding particularly remarkable.

The discovery was made possible by combining observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawai'i. The research was led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, and is described in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Industry observers note that gemini North is one of the two telescopes that make up the International Gemini Observatory. Operated by NSF NOIRLab, the observatory is an international partnership led by the U.S. National Science Foundation, with participation from Canada, Chile, Brazil, Argentina, and the Republic of Korea.

How Giant Black Holes Formed in the Early Universe.

In a recent development, during the first billion years after the Major Bang, the Universe underwent a period of extraordinary transformation. Vast concentrations of invisible matter, known as dark matter halos, collapsed under gravity. The earliest galaxies began producing stars, while increasingly massive galaxies developed the first supermassive black holes at their centers.

In a recent development, as galaxies passed near one another, collided, and sometimes merged, enormous quantities of gas and stars became available to feed their central black holes. Some of the material falling toward these black holes released tremendous amounts of energy. This process, known as accretion, could generate radiation so intense that the glowing region surrounding a black hole outshone every star in its host galaxy.

Astronomers call these extraordinarily luminous objects quasars.

Industry observers note that because galaxy encounters and mergers occur frequently throughout the Universe, researchers expect many quasars to exist in pairs separated by distances smaller than the typical diameter of a galaxy. Yet detecting these systems has remained a major challenge.

According to recent reports, one reason is that a supermassive black hole spends only a relatively brief period in its bright "quasar phase." Another is the enormous distance separating ancient quasars from Earth, which makes them appear extremely faint to ground-based telescopes. Even when both objects are visible, their close proximity can make it difficult to distinguish one from the other.

Two Monster Black Holes That Grew Too Massive, Too Fast.

Recent findings suggest that nāpōwawāʻenakaulua stands out because it is only the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn. More importantly, its two black holes were already so enormous at such an early stage of cosmic history that existing theories cannot definitively explain their growth.

The black holes are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, equivalent to about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way. One has an estimated mass of 1.5 billion Suns, while the other weighs approximately 400 million solar masses.

Astronomers see the pair as it appeared only 900 million years after the Massive Bang, when the Universe was still populated by relatively young stars, galaxies, and black holes. Finding two black holes comparable in mass to many present-day supermassive black holes at this early time raises difficult questions about how quickly the first enormous cosmic structures could assemble.

Recent findings suggest that "There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two," claims Onorato. "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.".

In a recent development, the pair's Hawaiian name reflects the extraordinary forces involved. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua translates to "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.".

The name was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program, a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai'i's Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College).[1].

How James Webb and Gemini North Revealed the Hidden Pair.

In a recent development, the discovery began with data collected by the Aether survey, a JWST research program designed to identify and characterize objects from the early Universe. The project is led by Emanuele Paolo Farina, an Associate Scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini.

It has been revealed that using JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit, the survey assembled observations of 200 quasars. That sample represents approximately 43% of all quasars known from this period of cosmic history.

It has been revealed that while visually examining the survey data, researchers noticed something unexpected. A previously identified quasar, J1602+4228A, appeared to have a companion.

According to recent reports, to investigate, the team turned to Gemini North's Gemini Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GNIRS). These observations allowed astronomers to distinguish the two quasars individually, providing crucial evidence about the nature of the system.

Industry observers note that obtaining those measurements was an exceptional achievement. The objects are separated by such a small apparent distance, and the companion J1602+4228B is so faint, that resolving them with a telescope on Earth was expected to be nearly impossible.

According to recent reports, fortunately, the researchers benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea. Clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions enabled them to gather the necessary observations in just two nights.

"The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights," says Onorato.

The team also used Gemini North's Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to gather additional information about the system and refine their understanding of the two quasars.[2].

A Newly introduced Clue to the Universe's First Giant Galaxies.

It has been revealed that exactly how Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua formed remains unknown. However, the researchers believe its extraordinary properties could point to an unusually dense concentration of matter in the early Universe.

In such an environment, frequent interactions between young galaxies may have provided enormous supplies of gas, simultaneously accelerating the birth of stars and fueling rapid growth of the black holes at their centers.

If this interpretation is correct, the quasar pair could help scientists understand how the earliest massive galaxies developed alongside their central supermassive black holes.

It has been revealed that "Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," indicates Onorato. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peacock's Dig is just one Parks and Recreation reunion after another.

It has been revealed that the archaeological comedy is co-created by Amy Poehler and Mike Schur, who both worked together on Parks and Recreation. Schur co-created that series with Greg Daniels, and Poehler led the show as waffle-loving civil servant Leslie Knope.

However, Poehler and Schur's collaboration isn't the only spark of Parks and Recreation magic you'll find in Dig. In a blink-and-you'll-miss-it moment, Dig also features a cameo from none other than Rashida Jones, who plays Leslie's best friend, nurse Ann Perkins, in Parks and Recreation.

Jones' appearance occurs in episode 5, when she pops up as a woman taking a photo of archaeologists Elise (Poehler) and Neville (Hugh Laurie) at a beachside restaurant. My Parks-loving self has never rewound a scene so fast to make sure my eyes weren't deceiving me.

It has been revealed that according to Schur, the cameo came about due to proximity. Dig shot in Italy and Greece, and Jones is semi-permanently located in London. Schur, Poehler, and Jones, who have been friends since even before working together on Parks and Recreation, were communicating with one another during production.

Sources indicate that "We were just texting with [Jones], and we were like, 'It's not that long a flight. What if you just hopped over here and hung out with us at this hotel we're staying at?'" Schur told Mashable over Zoom. "Then once she was there, it was a very quick jump to, 'You've got to just go into the show. You've got to pop in for a scene.'".

From there, Schur, Poehler, and Jones came up with the quick photo cameo.

In a recent development, "That's part of the fun of knowing people and working together for a really long time, is you do silly things like that," Schur recalled. "It was really fun, and she was totally game for it.".

The highlight of the scene comes right after Jones exits, when Elise casually remarks, "She's very pretty.".

Industry observers note that for Parks and Recreation fans, the compliment instantly recalls Leslie's non-stop raves over Ann's beauty, whether it's calling her a "beautiful tropical fish" or a "poetic, noble land-mermaid." It's a sweet reminder of one of TV's most enduring female friendships, and it's right at home in Dig, which is full of sweet female friendships in its own right. Plus, according to Schur, the remark was completely improvised by Poehler.

"It was a very smart little mini gift to the folks who were fans of that show who will enjoy seeing them back together again," Schur stated.

#162000. Tech Report: Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s Beach

Tech Report: Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s Beach

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A volcanic eruption just off the southeast shore of the Pacific island has reshaped the coast, but it’s unclear how long the new land will survive.
  • A volcanic eruption in the shallows near Iwo Jima has extended the Japanese island’s famed black sand beaches, at least temporarily.
  • Signs of unrest began in late October 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A volcanic eruption just off the southeast shore of the Pacific island has reshaped the coast, but it’s unclear how long the new land will survive.

A volcanic eruption in the shallows near Iwo Jima has extended the Japanese island’s famed black sand beaches, at least temporarily.

Signs of unrest began in late October 2026. On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agency reported that the first photographs of the eruption were captured. Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations.

Industry observers note that the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet. On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right). A shortwave-infrared signature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange. A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floating pumice stretches across the water in the same direction.

According to recent reports, A false-color backscatter radar image from the NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption. On October 28, despite heavy cloud cover, the radar detected a large disturbance in the water in the same area that erupted in December 2023. When the clouds cleared in early November, the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on NASA and NOAA satellites also captured signs of the ongoing eruption’s volcanic plumes and infrared signature.

Japan’s Coast Guard released a report on November 16 confirming the formation of fresh land connected to the pre-existing beach. The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields. That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent. The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of the bloodiest battles in the history of the U.S. Marines.

According to recent reports, the location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists. In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.

How long the newly introduced land will persist remains an open question. New land created by the 2023 eruption succumbed to wave action after just a few weeks, Slayback said. New land on volcanic islands has persisted more than a decade only a handful of times in recent times, including at Capelinhos, Surtsey, McDonald Island, and Home Reef, he added. “I imagine we’ll see this new land wash away within a few months,” he said. “But we’ll have to wait and see.”.

Among the scientists watching closely is James Garvin, the chief scientist at Goddard and a geologist with a long-standing interest in how underwater volcanic eruptions create newly introduced islands and other landforms.

It has been revealed that typically, tephra-dominated eruptions like this form new land that is swiftly “attacked” by ocean waves and other hydrologic forces, Garvin explained. An exception is when the eruption also injects certain types of lava that “cement” the ash into stronger material. “If we do see injection of basaltic-andesitic lava within the new materials, then it’s possible the new land could follow a pattern different from what we monitored in 2023,” he noted.

In a recent development, NISAR will be especially valuable for tracking the site, Garvin remarked, because it makes frequent, high-resolution interferometric observations through clouds and can show whether the new land erodes, subsides, or grows. The satellite has already recorded major changes at the eruption site between October 28 and November 11.

According to recent reports, NASA scientists will also analyze sub-meter-resolution imagery from commercial satellites through NASA’s Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program. These images can reveal subtle deformation features like rilles, fractures, and cracks that offer clues about the stability of the fresh land.

In a recent development, both Slayback and Garvin have studied fresh volcanic land before. They were part of a team that monitored new land in the Kingdom of Tonga after an eruption in the Southwest Pacific but before most of it was obliterated during the highly explosive Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha‘apai caldera collapse and eruption in January 2022.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Adam Voiland.

#161999. This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
